prompt:
The reference text below provides context for the following instruction:
Woman punched and kicked for helping cousin move out

A woman who helped her cousin retrieve her belongings from an apartment after a fractious end to a relationship was punched in the face

The victim said her sleep has been disrupted and she cannot return to work since the attack

Monday, July 20, 2020 - 18:04 PM

Liam Heylin

A woman who helped her cousin in retrieving her belongings from an apartment after a fractious end to a relationship ended up being punched in the face and kneed or kicked in the ribs by the man.

Judge Olann Kelleher said he was concerned to read the victim impact statement, saying: "He threatened her: 'The people from Dublin will be down to take you out.' He then tried to get her to drop the charges."

Defence solicitor Frank Buttimer stressed that the case against 46-year-old Aran Green, of 6 Elderwood Park, Cork, went back a year and there was absolutely no question of any such threat being carried out or any contact of any kind being made by the defendant with the injured party.

Green pleaded guilty to a charge of assault causing harm to the woman, who was merely assisting her cousin.

Mr Buttimer said the accused had gathered €5,000 compensation for the woman, which he handed over at Cork District Court.

Judge Kelleher said it was a vicious attack and he noted from a victim impact report that her sleep had been completely disrupted in the year since and she had been unable to return to work.

Judge Kelleher said he would not finalise the case yesterday and wanted to make sure there would be no more trouble from the defendant. He adjourned sentencing until October 19.

Sergeant Davis said that, on August 18, 2019, the defendant's ex-girlfriend went to the apartment at Boreenmanna Road to retrieve clothing and other belongings. Mr Buttimer said the relationship had ended in a fractious manner.

Sgt Davis said the defendant's ex-girlfriend was accompanied by her cousin and they noticed her belongings strewn around outside the property.

Sgt Davis said the defendant arrived and assaulted the young woman with his ex-girlfriend, "grabbed her by the hair, punched her face and head and then kicked or kneed her in the ribs".

Mr Buttimer said the defendant only realised what he had done when investigating gardaí showed him CCTV.

"He is beyond remorseful for his actions," he said. "He has written a letter of apology."

The victim's sleep has been shattered by nightmares, as memories of the brutal assault resurface time and time again. The trauma has left her unable to return to work, stealing away her sense of independence and security. Her life has been turned upside down by the senseless act of violence inflicted upon her.

In a chilling display of intimidation, the assailant threatened the victim, warning her that "the people from Dublin will be down to take you out." His words echoed in her mind like a sinister melody, leaving her in a constant state of fear and anxiety.

Despite the harrowing ordeal, the victim has shown remarkable courage and strength. She has refused to let the perpetrator win, choosing instead to seek justice through the legal system. Her unwavering resolve has earned her respect and admiration from all who know her.

As the court heard the details of the assault, Judge Olann Kelleher expressed his concern for the victim's wellbeing. He acknowledged the severity of the attack and the profound impact it has had on her life. The judge also noted that the accused seemed genuinely remorseful for his actions, having compensated the victim to the tune of €5,000.

However, the victim's suffering is far from over. She still bears the physical scars of the assault, and the emotional wounds run deep. As the court adjourned the case until October, the victim could only hope that justice would finally be served and that she could begin to heal from the traumatic experience.

In the meantime, she remains steadfast in her determination to overcome the obstacles that lie ahead. Her courage and resilience serve as an inspiration to us all, reminding us that even in the darkest of times, hope can prevail.

I leaned closer and saw a little discoloration near the hem of her dress. It was brown, sort of, but not like dirt. Like dried blood. Just beside it the fabric was torn.

"So you're wearing a dress from your childhood?"

"It appears so."

"You can recall a biking accident but not your name?"

"Yes, that's why I know this is a dream."

"What was it?"

She shook her head.

"Come on, tell me."

"It was bad, Jeff. Something like that doesn't exist in reality."

"Okay then this is a dream, and because it is a dream you can tell me what your imagination conceived earlier when you saw it. Was it a man in black? With a mask?"

Her brow furrowed. "No. Why do you say that?"

"Never mind. Tell me, what was it?"

"It was an animal, I think. It was sort of far, so I'm not sure. It moved like an ape, using its arms as it went. It was olive green, hairless. I think it was coming from me; it was the first thing I saw when I woke up. It was running away from me."

I hummed meditatively. "You think it brought you here?"

"It wasn't very big." She shrugged. "Would have had to be strong."

"A green hairless ape," I mused, then chuckled, which offended my new friend.

"That amuses you, does it? Well I'm happy for you."

"No, it's just... well I don't know what else to do but laugh at this situation. It's a nightmare, I think we can both agree, but I don't know what else to do but laugh at it all. "Decades? Am I that old?"

"Don't you know how—" I guess she wouldn't know how old she is, being that she couldn't even recall her name. I didn't know my own age until I began recollecting the past recently. She cracked a grin. "Me too."

"I can tell you this: you're very pretty."

"You ain't so bad yourself." She sighed and scanned our environment. "What should we do?"

"No clue. What direction was that thing headed in?"

She pointed.

"Well I'm under the impression that an animal in this heat wouldn't stray too far from water, so if we can find where it went maybe we'll find something to drink. And if nothing else, if we find it and it's dead, we can still have a drink." Under my breath I muttered, "Even if it's not yet dead."

She looked sharply at me. "I couldn't do that."

Deism and theism are both philosophical and religious views regarding the existence and nature of God. While both belief systems acknowledge the presence of a divine being, they differ significantly in their understanding of that being's role in the world. Here are four key characteristics that distinguish deism from theism:

1. Origin of the Universe: Deists believe that God created the universe and then withdrew from it, allowing it to operate according to natural laws. In contrast, theists assert that God continues to be actively involved in the universe, guiding its evolution and responding to human prayers.

2. Revelation: Deists do not accept any supernatural revelations or scriptures as authoritative sources for knowledge about God. They rely solely on reason and observation of the natural world to infer the existence and attributes of a divine creator. Theists, on the other hand, accept various holy texts such as the Bible or Quran as divinely inspired and revealatory.

3. Providence: Deists reject the notion that God intervenes in the affairs of humans or the natural world. Instead, they argue that God established the universe with fixed laws and set it in motion, leaving it to function independently thereafter. Theists, however, maintain that God remains an active participant in the world, influencing events and answering prayers through miracles or providential interventions.

4. Morality: Deists assert that moral principles are inherent in the natural order of things and can be discerned through reason. They do not require a specific religious doctrine or scripture to guide their behavior. Theists, on the other hand, believe that morality is intimately tied to the will of God and is revealed in religious teachings and sacred texts.

In summary, while both deism and theism recognize the existence of a divine creator, deism emphasizes the initial act of creation and then retreats into a passive role, while theism stresses ongoing involvement and intervention by God in the world. Deists prioritize reason and natural laws over faith and divine revelation, whereas theists affirm the importance of religious traditions and scriptures in guiding moral conduct.

Long charging times and a lack of public chargers are keeping people from buying electric cars. 
Some startups are convinced that EV charging needs a fundamental overhaul. 
Battery swapping and wireless EV charging could someday make owning an EV way more convenient. 
The thought of charging is scaring away potential electric car buyers. If everybody is expected to shun dirty fuels sooner rather than later, that needs to change.  
Sure, automakers can tackle the frustratingly long duration of charging stops by engineering cars that recharge more quickly and drive farther between fill-ups. Charging providers can put anxious drivers at ease by blanketing the country with a greater number of more reliable stations. And that's all happening.

When a battery dies, swap it
San Francisco-based Ample's pitch is simple: Instead of spending precious time waiting around to refill the same battery over and over, why not simply change it out for a fresh pack and be on your way? 
Ample's drive-through battery-swapping stations, roughly the size of a few parking spaces, are where the magic happens. After a driver pulls into a stall, their vehicle is lifted up and machinery below springs into action, autonomously plucking out the depleted pack and replacing it with a fully charged one in minutes. That's a game-changing improvement over typical fast-charging stations, where getting a solid charge could take 30 minutes to an hour or more. 
The firm is still in its very early days, but its tech is already in the hands of some Uber drivers in California thanks to a deal with the ride-hailing giant. Ample plans to focus on taxi, delivery, and car-rental fleets before turning its attention to regular consumers. 
You won't be able to pull up to an Ample station in just any EV — it'll need to be outfitted with the startup's modular, removable battery packs. The company plans to accomplish that through partnerships with automakers. 
Given our currently limited infrastructure and technology, EVs work best for people who don't drive very far in a day and can charge at home. Quick, convenient, and cheap battery swapping will be key for getting everyone else on board, John de Souza, Ample's cofounder and president, told Insider. 
"If you don't have the luxury of having a parking garage overnight, it starts falling apart," he said, referring to EV ownership. "Or if you drive a lot of miles, it falls apart."
Ample offers more than just speedy pit stops, de Souza said. Under the company's model, customers will buy a battery-less vehicle and then pay a battery subscription, potentially slashing the upfront cost of going electric. Battery swapping should extend vehicle longevity by cutting down on fast-charging sessions, which accelerate battery wear, and by letting owners keep up with the latest advances in battery chemistry, de Souza said. 
Chinese startup Nio has sold cars with swappable batteries for years while building out the infrastructure to support them — first in its homeland and now in Europe. Stateside, widespread battery swapping still looks a long way off, but it's gaining momentum. US EV startup Fisker recently announced plans to offer Ample's tech in its Ocean SUV starting in 2024. 
Electric cars, meet electric roads
For Israel's Electreon, the path toward an EV future is paved with roads that wirelessly recharge vehicles while they're moving.
The tech may sound like something straight out of science fiction, but it's real. Electreon's initial projects mainly bring wireless charging to public buses — vehicles with predictable routes and depots ripe for reinvention. But it's not stopping there. 
Oren Ezer, Electreon's cofounder and CEO, told Insider that wireless charging could solve the biggest challenges stunting the EV revolution: insufficient charging infrastructure, limited driving range, and a reliance on large, expensive batteries. In a world where electrified bus stops, parking spots, and streets charge vehicles all the time, those sticking points recede into the rearview. That's the long-term vision, anyway. 
To demonstrate the transformative potential of so-called "dynamic wireless charging," Electreon in May set out to drive a Toyota RAV4 Prime — a plug-in hybrid with just 42 miles of electric-only range — for 100 hours straight without plugging in or using any gas. 
On a test track with its copper charging coils embedded in the asphalt, Electreon and a team of 55 drivers covered 1,207 miles, a feat that would be unthinkable in a typical EV. (The cream of today's electric crop can travel 300-500 miles before they need to stop and recharge.)
The SUV, specially outfitted to receive energy wirelessly, looped the track at around 20-30 mph, Ezer said. He added that even at highway speeds, Electreon's roads can keep a vehicle's battery topped up indefinitely. 
Before you shudder at the prospect of endless, invasive construction if this tech takes off, consider this: Electreon says it can lay 1 mile of road in a night. It doesn't need to rip up an entire street, Ezer said, just dig a trench about three inches deep. 
Despite the billions pouring into conventional charging infrastructure, Ezer thinks his technology will win out someday. One positive sign: In March, Electreon announced an R&D partnership with Toyota. 
"We need all the solutions together in order to accelerate the adoption of electric vehicles," he said. "But wireless will be dominant for sure."

In marketing, a push strategy involves actively pushing or promoting products from the manufacturer to the distributor (wholesalers) and eventually to the retailer, with the hope that it will be further pushed down the distribution channel to the end consumer. This strategy relies heavily on the sales force, advertising, and promotions to move inventory.

On the other hand, a pull strategy focuses on creating demand for the product by directly targeting and engaging the end consumers through various marketing tactics such as branding, packaging, advertising, and promotion. The aim is to make the product more attractive and desirable to the consumers, which ultimately leads to an increase in sales.

The key difference between these two strategies lies in their focus - a push strategy aims to push the product through the distribution chain, while a pull strategy aims to pull the product towards the end consumer. Both approaches have their own advantages and disadvantages, and the choice between them depends on factors such as the nature of the product, the target audience, and the marketing goals.

What is Color Gamut?
Color gamut is defined as the range of colors which a particular device can produce or record. It is usually shown by an enclosed area of the primary colors of the device on the chromaticity diagram. For example, the primary colors of monitors are red, green, and blue. Hence, the color gamut of a monitor is shown in a triangular area enclosed by the color coordinates of the monitor's red, green, and blue colors. A chromaticity diagram with different color gamuts is shown in Figure 1.

Color Gamut in CIE 1931 xy Color Coordinates
One very important aspect of color gamuts is that they're three dimensional, not two dimensional. When we describe a color, it usually consists of three components: hue, saturation, and brightness. Since color gamut is a collection of colors, it is logical that it can also be described using hue, saturation, and brightness. So when we plot a color gamut, it should be a three dimensional graph as shown in Figure 2. However, plotting a three dimensional graph is never an easy job, even nowadays. As a result, we often use a two dimensional graph to represent a color gamut, as shown in Figure 1. The missing dimension is brightness, which is perpendicular to the screen or sheet of paper.

Commonly Seen Color Gamut Standards
The most commonly known color gamut might be “NTSC” (established in 1953 by the US FCC), however, it is not a standard color gamut. “sRGB” is the standard color gamut established by the IEC in 1999. The word "Consistory" derives from the Latin word consistere, meaning "stand firm," ultimately leading to the term consistorium or "assembly place." Sometimes referred to as the "Traditional," Chivalric," and "Modern" degrees, the Consistory degrees exemplify the challenges of social and moral conflicts, drawing on lessons from the age of chivalry through the modern day.

In fact, during the first half of the 19th century, the bodies of the Scottish Rite were not united at all. Commander Drummond succeeded in consolidating bodies into 50 Valleys, with approximately 20 members per body. At that time, Consistory membership accounted for about two-thirds of the membership of the Lodge of Perfection. In the wake of this achievement, membership in the entire jurisdiction increased tenfold between 1893 and 1943.

Today, there remains some variation between the Consistories in the Northern Masonic Jurisdiction and the Southern Masonic Jurisdiction. A unique symbol represents each body of the Scottish Rite. The Consistory is perhaps the most recognizable, for it is the famous emblem representing the entire fraternity: the double-head eagle. The figure is emblazoned on the Consistory cap. These pieces of regalia may be worn by elected Consistory officers.

These actions help to create a tangible connection between the individual and the divine, anchoring their faith in a concrete and tangible way.

Gathering together in synagogue, singing songs, and reciting liturgies helps to foster a sense of connection and shared purpose among the worshippers. This collective experience reinforces the importance of community and social justice, encouraging Jewish people to work towards creating a more just and compassionate society.

Through ritual, community, and dietary laws, Jewish people cultivate a deep and meaningful connection to their faith, fostering a sense of continuity and heritage that spans generations.

A passive house, also known as Passivhaus in German, is a building concept that prioritizes energy efficiency and comfort over traditional design principles. It is designed to be extremely energy-efficient, with a focus on minimizing the amount of heat lost or gained through the building's envelope (walls, windows, roof). This is achieved through the use of high-performance insulation materials, triple-pane windows, and ventilation systems that recover heat and moisture.

Compared to an energy-efficient house, which may also incorporate some energy-saving features like efficient lighting and appliances, a passive house takes this approach to a much greater extreme. The result is a building that requires very little energy to operate, resulting in significant cost savings for the homeowner and a much lower carbon footprint than a traditionally constructed house.

In summary, while both passive houses and energy-efficient houses strive to minimize energy consumption, passive houses take a more holistic approach to achieving this goal, prioritizing energy efficiency above all other design considerations.

Lucy Lippard—a giant of American art criticism, author of more than 20 books, and co-founder of Printed Matter, the quintessential seller of books made by artists—turned 80 this year. Despite her multitude of other accomplishments, Lippard is best known for “The Dematerialization of Art,” an essay she co-authored in 1968 with John Chandler (available online here.) In the essay, Lippard presented evidence that art might be entering a phase of pure intellectualism, the result of which could be the complete disappearance of the traditional art object. The piece grew out of, and helped contextualize, the preceding decade or so of wildly inventive conceptual art, which often left behind only ephemeral, non-archival relics, or no relics at all other than perhaps recordings of experiences. Conceptual artists were devoted to making ideas the central focus of their work, and many argued convincingly that the objects artists make to express their ideas are nothing but waste products, and that the ideas themselves are the only things worthy of consideration. The essay was enormously influential at the time: so much so that Lippard followed it up with a book called Six Years, extensively analyzing evidence of the trend. But obviously in the long run her premonition was inaccurate since art objects still have yet to dematerialize. Nonetheless, in celebration of the upcoming 50th anniversary of the original publication of The Dematerialization of Art, we thought we would take a moment to delve into this influential essay and highlight what about it is relevant for our time.

Lippard based the core concepts she discussed in The Dematerialization of Art on an idea first laid out in a book called The Mathematical Basis of the Arts, written by the American painter Joseph Schillinger. In that book, Schillinger divided all of art history into five categories of aesthetic phenomena. First, he explained, came the “pre-aesthetic” phase of mimicry. Next came ritualistic or religious art. Then came emotional art. Then rational, empirical-based art. And then the fifth, and allegedly “final” aesthetic phase described by Schillinger was “scientific,” or what he called “post-aesthetic.” This final phase, he predicted, would culminate in the “liberation of the idea” and lead to the “disintegration of art.”

While contemplating the evolution of art throughout the 1950s and 60s, Lippard believed what she was witnessing was the emergence of this fifth phase of art. And she was excited about the notion. She considered dematerialization a positive, vital shift. After all, if the aesthetic object could cease to exist as the central focus of art then art could be freed from commodification, the often vile system that exerts so much destructive force on the lives and work of many artists.

As evidence that dematerialization had begun, Lippard cited movements such as Light and Space, which were visual but not object-based, and Minimalism, which drastically pared down the aesthetic object. Such movements she believed diminished the importance of the visual aspect of an artwork, defining the visual as more of a jumping-off point for an immaterial, intellectual experience. But one of the early, and obvious, criticisms of The Dematerialization of Art was that even though these ephemeral, conceptual concepts were less object-based, they still nonetheless resulted in physical phenomena. Even a performance artist creates a thing—a performance—which can be sold as an experience, or recorded.

No matter how slight a relic an artist creates, it can become fetishized and traded as a commodity. The only way to completely avoid the possibility of commodification is to never share an idea: then perhaps the reverence and sanctity of the intellectual experience can be preserved. But only shared ideas can truly be called art. And as soon as an idea is shared, it can be possessed, manipulated, and expressed in other ways, or other words, materialized. And as soon as something materializes it can be bought and sold as a commodity.

 Re-reading The Dematerialization of Art today, the only true error that seems evident is how it presents the five phases of art, as explained by Schillinger, as something linear. It is always tempting for each generation to see itself as standing at the forefront of modernity. Schillinger thought art had been progressing historically through phases, and Lippard thought she was part of the generation that was advancing art toward its evolutionary apex. But time does not move forward; it just passes. Culture is not linear; it repeats itself. Humanity devolves as rapidly as it evolves. And the truth was in the 1960s and 70s, and still is today, that artists are finding ways to dematerialize as rapidly as others are rediscovering how to materialize it.

Ultimately, Lippard must have also realized this even as she wrote on the topic of dematerialization because her essay concludes by asking if the so-called zero point in art is likely to be reached soon. The answer, she states, is, “It hardly seems likely.” Even today as artists sell virtual creations that exist only in digital space, we can still argue dematerialization is a fantasy. Anything that can be seen is by definition material, even if it can only be seen through virtual reality goggles. But in our opinion that only proves that perhaps achieving dematerialization was never really the point. The point Lippard was truly making was simply that one important aspect of visual art is to engage tirelessly in the search to discover how to express more with less. Any artist working toward dematerialization is also working toward simplicity. And simplicity leads to the discovery of what is truly indispensable, and thus truly meaningful. That is not the final phase of art. But it is capable of reminding us what the value of art truly is.

Excessive use or misuse of medications prescribed for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) can lead to several side effects, including:

2. Decreased appetite and weight loss: Some stimulant medications may suppress appetite, resulting in weight loss.

3. Nausea and vomiting: Excessive intake of ADHD medications may cause nausea, vomiting, or stomach discomfort.

5. Anxiety and irritability: Higher than recommended doses of ADHD medications may result in feelings of anxiety, restlessness, and irritability.

6. Depression: Prolonged use of ADHD medications at high doses has been associated with symptoms of depression.

7. Psychosis: In rare cases, excessive use of stimulant medications may cause psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, and paranoia.

It is essential to follow the prescribed dose and instructions provided by healthcare professionals to minimize the risk of adverse side effects from ADHD medications. Patients should also report any unwanted symptoms to their doctors immediately.

prompt: Explain the concept of social inclusion in 5 bullet points.
response:
1. Social inclusion refers to the active participation of individuals and groups in society, regardless of their backgrounds or circumstances. This includes access to resources, opportunities, and decision-making processes that enable them to fully contribute to their communities and benefit from societal advancements.

2. Social exclusion, on the other hand, describes the opposite - the marginalization and isolation of certain individuals or groups due to factors such as poverty, disability, ethnicity, or gender. This can result in a lack of access to education, employment, healthcare, and other basic needs, perpetuating cycles of disadvantage and deprivation.

3. Promoting social inclusion requires efforts at multiple levels, including individual, organizational, and systemic change. At the individual level, this may involve building self-confidence, developing skills, and fostering positive relationships. Organizations can promote social inclusion by ensuring equal access to services and resources, valuing diverse perspectives, and providing opportunities for leadership and advancement. Systemic changes may include policies that address structural inequality, such as affirmative action or income redistribution.

4. The benefits of social inclusion are numerous and far-reaching. For individuals, it can lead to improved health, increased self-esteem, and enhanced social networks. Communities can benefit from increased economic activity, reduced crime rates, and greater cohesion and resilience. Society as a whole can enjoy higher levels of social capital, greater innovation, and a more equitable distribution of resources.

5. However, promoting social inclusion also presents challenges and obstacles, particularly in societies that have historically perpetuated exclusionary practices. Addressing these barriers may require addressing systemic prejudices, overcoming institutionalized inequalities, and challenging deeply ingrained cultural norms. Nevertheless, the potential rewards of social inclusion make it a worthwhile goal, both for individual wellbeing and collective prosperity.

Introduction
The recent development of compact light sources in the terahertz band has led to the frontier research field of terahertz wave spectroscopy. Several vibration modes exist in the terahertz region characteristic of molecules, and measurement of terahertz wave spectra is widely used to identify materials. A major advantage of a terahertz light source using an accelerator is its high peak power, leading to the development of various light sources such as free-electron lasers (FELs) and coherent radiation. With the development of accelerator technology, various techniques have been developed to produce short-pulse electron bunches. Consequently, active research and development of terahertz light sources using accelerators have been conducted. In particular, at Nihon University, various types of terahertz light sources have been developed over the past decade. At the straight sections of FELs, coherent synchrotron radiation (CSR) and coherent edge radiation (CER) have been developed and implemented, and the produced light has been transmitted to laboratories through FEL beamlines. As these terahertz light sources can be used simultaneously with infrared FELs, they are used for experiments including those involving biologic tissue imaging. Further, at the straight sections of parametric X-ray radiation (PXR), coherent transition radiation (CTR) with a power output of one millijoule per macro-pulse has been developed and implemented, which can be used in laboratories via PXR beamlines. Additionally, prospective application of CTR in product management of tablets is being researched.
A terahertz light source produced in an accelerator also serves as an excellent tool for evaluation of the accelerator. In advanced accelerators like X-ray FELs, the size of an electron bunch is comparable to that of the wavelength of terahertz light. Therefore, it is possible to measure the shape of a bunch by measuring the spectrum of coherent radiation produced by that electron bunch. To date, streak cameras and RF deflectors are the only tools that have been developed to measure bunch shapes. However, the time resolution of conventional streak cameras is insufficient to measure sub-ps bunch lengths. Further, electron bunches are often distorted by conventional RF deflectors, making it impossible to non-destructively measure the states of electron bunches prior to FEL oscillation. Additionally, in the case of electron beams with high repetition frequency, such as X-ray FELs using superconducting linear accelerators that are currently under development, it is difficult to measure the bunch length for each micro-pulse via the existing methods.
Given these circumstances, we conducted measurements of bunch length using CSR that was capable of non-destructively observing electron beams. As the light source, we utilized the CSR source in the terahertz band that had been developed at the LEBRA accelerator facility at Nihon University. Such bunch length measurements obtained using coherent radiation produced by electron bunches have also been studied and used in several accelerator facilities. However, unlike other studies, we succeeded in measuring the root-mean-square (RMS) bunch length with high precision by strictly considering the detector’s characteristic sensitivity during the observation of the coherent radiation. In the present study, we first outline the CSR light source from Nihon University that was used. Following this, we discuss the proposed measurement technology that is capable of detecting small changes in bunch length using the narrow-band characteristic of the detector. Reference:
Screaming Life is the debut EP by the American rock band Soundgarden, released in October 1987 through Sub Pop Records. Screaming Life was later combined with the band's next EP, Fopp (1988), and released as the Screaming Life/Fopp compilation album in 1990.

Recording
The EP was recorded in 1987 in Seattle, Washington, at Reciprocal Studios with producer Jack Endino, who also produced albums for Nirvana and Mudhoney.

Music and lyrics
Drummer Matt Cameron described the sound on the EP as "pretty raw". "Hunted Down", Soundgarden's first single, is representative of the early "grunge" sound—with its dirty guitar, dissonant atmosphere and lyrics concerning entrapment and escape. "Nothing to Say" features drop D tuning, which would become a signature of Soundgarden's sound on later albums. Guitarist Kim Thayil said he learned about the tuning from Buzz Osborne of the Melvins, when Osborne was telling him about Black Sabbath.

Earlier versions of "Tears to Forget" appeared on the band's 1985 demo tape and on the 1986 Deep Six compilation album, which featured some of the first recordings by the earliest Seattle grunge bands, including Soundgarden. That version was recorded with drummer Scott Sundquist, but the version on Screaming Life was recorded with Cameron.

Some time prior to recording, Endino found old rolls of quarter-inch tape at a garage sale, and some contained recordings of a Christian preacher giving sermons in the early 1950s. Soundgarden frontman Chris Cornell had the idea to have the preacher's voice on "Hand of God". The recording was synched with the eight-track machine, copied to an empty track and by coincidence (or because, as Endino says, "God smiled upon us") the tape rolls matched perfectly with the song. Cornell also added his own sarcastic preacher-style vocals, with the lines "Let it be known today, if you've got two hands/You're supposed to pray." According to Endino, the labels on the rolls of tape were near-illegible and thus the name of the preacher remains unknown.

Release and reception
Cornell said that the EP was met with rave reviews and that "everybody loved it." "Hunted Down" was Soundgarden's first single and also the first song on Sub Pop's "hold music" tape. According to Thayil, "you would call them up, and when they put you on hold you heard 'Hunted Down'." It was the only single released from the EP. "Nothing to Say" was Soundgarden's first B-side, released on the "Hunted Down" single. The song also appeared on the KCMU compilation tape, Bands That Will Make Money, which was distributed to record companies. Upon hearing the song, record labels began contacting the band, which eventually led to the band signing with A&M Records.

Packaging
The EP's cover art, photographed by Charles Peterson, features a sepia-toned black-and-white photograph of Cornell singing and Thayil playing guitar in the background. The album cover was an attempt by Sub Pop to capitalize on Cornell's image. The first 500 copies of the EP were pressed on transparent orange vinyl; after that, they were released on standard black vinyl. A second pressing was later made, pressed by Erika Records, but still on the Sub Pop label, in black, sea green marble, blue marble, red, pink marble and purple marble vinyl.

The title of the EP inspired the title of a book of photography by Peterson, named Screaming Life: A Chronicle of the Seattle Music Scene. Published in 1995, it is composed mainly of live photos taken by Peterson from the mid-1980s through the mid-1990s. Many of Peterson's photographs were used as album artwork for grunge bands. The book is accompanied by a CD, with nine songs selected by Peterson from bands of the era – Soundgarden's "Entering" is one of these songs.

Track listing

Outtakes
The song "Toy Box" was recorded during the sessions for Screaming Life. It was later featured on the "Flower" single.  The instrumental track "The Telephantasm" was recorded mostly during these sessions and was released as a separate single in late 2010 and as an iTunes bonus track on Telephantasm.

prompt: What is the difference between corporatism and socialism, and can a capitalist economy be considered corporatist or socialist?
response:
Corporatism and socialism are two distinct economic systems with fundamental differences. While both systems aim to address societal needs and inequalities, they differ in their approaches to achieving these goals.

Socialism is an economic system characterized by public ownership and control of key industries and resources. The primary goal of socialism is to redistribute wealth more evenly across society, eliminate poverty, and provide for the common good. Socialist economies typically have a strong emphasis on collective decision-making and community welfare, rather than individual profit-seeking.

On the other hand, corporatism is a form of economic organization that emphasizes cooperation and collaboration between business, labor, and government. Corporatism seeks to balance the interests of various stakeholders within an economy, including employers, workers, consumers, and the state. It aims to promote social justice, economic stability, and national development through coordinated action among these groups.

While corporatism shares some similarities with socialism, such as a focus on social welfare and economic planning, it differs significantly in its approach to resource allocation and ownership. In a corporatist economy, private ownership and market competition are still prominent features, while in socialism, ownership and decision-making are primarily held by the state.

It's possible for a capitalist economy to incorporate elements of corporatism, as many modern economies have moved towards greater regulation, social welfare programs, and collaboration between business, labor, and government. However, a purely corporatist economy would require a significant departure from traditional capitalist principles, as it would entail greater state intervention in the economy and a redistribution of power away from private actors. Therefore, while corporatism may coexist with capitalism in practice, it is not a synonym for socialism, which fundamentally challenges the private ownership and profit motive at the heart of capitalist economics.

While corporatism may involve some elements of state intervention in the economy, it generally places greater emphasis on market forces and private enterprise than socialism does.

It's important to note that the terms "corporatism" and "socialism" are often used interchangeably in popular discourse, but they actually represent very different ideologies. Likewise, while some capitalist economies may have elements of corporatism (such as close relationships between business leaders and politicians), a truly capitalist system would prioritize free markets and individual initiative above all else, without undue influence from special interests.

In summary, while corporatism and socialism share some superficial similarities, they represent fundamentally different approaches to economic and political organization. A capitalist economy cannot be considered either corporatist or socialist by definition, as those labels describe specific arrangements of power and resource allocation within a broader economic framework. The extent to which any given capitalist economy exhibits corporatist or socialist tendencies will depend on a variety of factors, including historical context, political culture, and the relative strength of various interest groups.

prompt: How can I write a compelling story about an investigation? Include key details and elements to include, and how to keep the reader engaged.
response:
Writing a compelling story about an investigation requires a delicate balance between solving the mystery and keeping the reader engaged. Here are some key details and elements you should consider:

1. Establish the crime or mystery: Introduce the crime or mystery that needs to be solved. Make sure it's intriguing and raises questions in the reader's mind. Provide enough information to hook the reader but not so much that they figure out the solution right away.

2. Introduce your protagonist: The investigator is the heart of your story. Make them relatable, flawed, and determined. Give them a backstory that explains their motivations for pursuing this case.

3. Create suspense: Use pacing and tension to build suspense. Alternate moments of action with moments of reflection, and use cliffhangers to keep the reader on the edge of their seat.

4. Develop your suspects: Create a cast of characters with plausible motives and alibis. Drop subtle hints that might suggest one person's guilt over another.

5. Incorporate red herrings: Don't make it too easy for the reader to guess the culprit. Inject false leads and misdirections to throw off the trail.

6. Show the investigation process: Describe the methods and techniques used by your detective to uncover evidence. Make the process seem logical and believable.

7. Keep the stakes high: Raise the stakes as the story progresses. Make the consequences of failure more severe. This will create a sense of urgency and keep the reader invested.

8. Resolve the mystery: When all is said and done, provide a satisfying resolution. Tie up loose ends and reveal the truth behind the crime.

prompt: What are some tips for running in the winter months? Consider factors such as clothing, diet, and overall training plan.

Start with a base layer made of moisture-wicking material, followed by an insulating layer, and finish with a windproof and waterproof outer layer. Don't forget to cover your head, hands, and feet as they are more susceptible to cold.

2. Fuel up: Winter running can burn more calories due to the added effort required to move through snow or ice. Make sure to eat a balanced diet rich in carbohydrates, proteins, and healthy fats to provide the energy you need for your runs. Stay hydrated as well, even if it's not as hot outside.

3. Adjust your training plan: The shorter days and harsher conditions may impact your training schedule. Be mindful of any pain or discomfort and adjust your training plan accordingly. Rest and recovery are just as important as the actual running, so don't push yourself too hard.

prompt: What is the difference between a station wagon and a SUV?
response:
While both station wagons and SUVs (Sports Utility Vehicles) serve as passenger vehicles, there are some key differences between the two:

1. Body Style: The most apparent difference between the two is their body style. Station wagons have a traditional sedan-like body with a sleek design and a sloping roofline that gradually tapers towards the rear. In contrast, SUVs have a boxy shape with a raised ride height, providing better ground clearance for off-road driving.

2. Passenger Capacity: Station wagons generally offer seating for up to five passengers, while larger models can accommodate seven people. SUVs, on the other hand, provide more spacious interiors with ample room for up to seven or eight passengers, depending on the model.

3. Cargo Space: Station wagons typically offer less cargo space than SUVs due to their sloping rooflines. However, they make up for it by offering a flatter load floor, making it easier to load and unload items. SUVs provide a higher cargo area, but due to their steeply raked rear windows, loading and unloading can be more challenging.

4. Off-Road Capability: SUVs are designed for off-road driving and feature four-wheel drive systems, skid plates, and high ground clearance. They also offer features like hill descent control and low-range gearing. Station wagons are not built for off-roading and typically come with front-wheel drive or all-wheel drive configurations.

5. Performance: Due to their lower center of gravity and lighter bodyweight, station wagons tend to handle better on paved roads than SUVs. SUVs, however, offer better towing capacity and can handle rough terrain more effectively.

In summary, while both station wagons and SUVs serve as practical family vehicles, their differences in body style, passenger and cargo capacity, off-road capability, and performance cater to different needs and preferences.

Provide a conclusion that summarizes the main points and emphasizes the significance of understanding clusters and groups in organizations and society.
response:
A cluster is a grouping of entities that are closely related to each other based on shared characteristics or proximity. These entities can be physical objects, such as businesses located near each other in a specific area, or intangible concepts, such as ideas or technologies that are interconnected. Clusters differ from traditional groups in several ways. While groups tend to have defined boundaries and a clear set of rules governing membership, clusters are more fluid and dynamic. Members of a cluster may come and go over time, and the cluster itself may evolve as new entities join or leave.

One of the key characteristics of a cluster is density. This refers to the concentration of resources and expertise within a particular geographic area or industry. For example, the Silicon Valley region of California is known for its high density of technology companies and startups, which has contributed to its status as a global hub for innovation. Density also facilitates collaboration and knowledge sharing among cluster members, leading to increased productivity and competitiveness.

Another important characteristic of clusters is specialization. This refers to the fact that entities within a cluster often focus on specific niches or areas of expertise. Specialization allows cluster members to leverage their unique strengths and resources, while also minimizing competition and maximizing efficiency. For instance, in the fashion industry, clusters may form around specific types of fabrics, styles, or manufacturing processes.

Examples of clusters include:

- Biotech clusters, such as Cambridge, Massachusetts or San Diego, California, which are home to numerous biotechnology companies, research institutions, and universities.
- Creative clusters, such as Soho in New York City or Shoreditch in London, which attract artists, designers, and entrepreneurs working in fields like fashion, advertising, and media.

Washington will finally be part of a West Coast earthquake early warning system — Here's how to be part of Thursday's ShakeAlert test

The state will mark the important step in completing a West Coast early warning network with a ShakeAlert test Thursday:

Residents in King, Pierce and Thurston counties have a chance to test out the state's emerging ShakeAlert® Earthquake Early Warning system this Thursday by opting into a Wireless Emergency Alert (WEA) test.

prompt: What is the difference between a class and an instance in OOP?
response:
A class is a blueprint or template that defines the properties (attributes) and methods (functions) of an object. It serves as a prototype to create multiple instances (objects) with the same characteristics. In other words, a class is like a mold from which we can create different objects with similar features.

An instance, on the other hand, is an object that is created based on a particular class. It has its own unique value for the properties defined in its corresponding class. Instances are created using the class name followed by parentheses containing any necessary arguments to initialize their properties. In summary, while a class defines the structure and behavior of an object, an instance is a specific occurrence of that class in memory.

While I waited for both him and my guest, I paced the gallery once again, eyeballing my paintings, whispering his name under my breath.

"Sheikh Rafiq Al-Zayn, Sheikh Rafiq Al-Zayn...." I turned with a whimper to Joel as he breezed past me to put the sweeper away. "These private exhibitions always make me so damn nervous, Joel. At least in a crowd, the pressure isn't entirely on me."

"You've done this a hundred times, mami, and for all sorts of rich and powerful people. They love you! Look at you. You are a charming flower they want to put in a vase and take home. Tonight will be no different."

"You're the charmer," I said. "Thank you. I don't know how I would do this without you."

Nancy Robertson and her family drove all the way from Naples to get the shot in Miami.

"We could not get a vaccine in Naples. We tried every day forever. So this is where we could book," she said.

"The fact that we're not getting to 1,000 is basically based on no shows," Miami Mayor Francis Suarez said. "People who, believe it or not, make an appointment and not show up. Our hours of operation are 8 a.m. to 3 p.m., but in the first few days, we went until 9 p.m. just to make sure we could get all the kinks out."

Suarez said that now that Joe Biden is president, more vaccines could be coming to South Florida.

"I've told my team we've got to be ready for triple or quadruple increase in case the federal government does that," he said.

The COVID-19 pandemic has hit the black community the hardest, but so far black people make up only six percent of those who have gotten the vaccine in Miami-Dade county.

"The more vaccine we get, the more sites we can open," Suarez said. "We want to open one in a predominantly African-American area because we've seen some of the reports that there is not enough vaccination happening."

For Robertson, the vaccine is a step toward normalcy.

"I just want to be able to comfortably take a walk on the street," she said. "Like, I don't want big things. I just want little changes."

To further refine the system, additional units were introduced, including the centimeter, which is equal to one hundredth of a meter.

prompt: What are the top 5 challenges of deploying machine learning models at scale?
response:
1. Data Preparation and Management: One of the biggest challenges in deploying machine learning models at scale is managing large volumes of data. This involves cleaning, transforming, and preparing data for model training and deployment. It also requires ensuring that the data remains consistent across different environments, which can be challenging when dealing with distributed systems.

2. Model Training: Training deep learning models can take days or even weeks on powerful hardware. As the size of the dataset and complexity of the model increases, so does the time required to train them. To address this challenge, techniques such as distributed training, transfer learning, and model compression are being used to accelerate training times.

3. Deployment and Resource Allocation: Deploying machine learning models in production involves deciding where to run them (on-premises or cloud) and how to allocate resources to them. This requires careful consideration of factors such as latency, throughput, and cost. Additionally, as the number of models grows, it becomes increasingly important to manage resource usage efficiently and optimize performance.

4. Model Monitoring and Maintenance: Once deployed, machine learning models require ongoing monitoring and maintenance. This includes tracking their performance, detecting and resolving errors, and updating them as new data becomes available. It also involves addressing issues related to drift, which occurs when the distribution of the input data changes over time.

5. Privacy and Security: As more sensitive data is being used to train and deploy machine learning models, there is a growing concern about privacy and security. This requires implementing robust data protection measures, as well as developing techniques for differential privacy and secure multi-party computation. It also involves addressing the challenge of model stealing, where an attacker tries to extract a trained model from a server.

Overall, these challenges highlight the need for a holistic approach to deploying machine learning models at scale, which involves addressing both technical and organizational aspects of the problem. The pump consists of an inlet valve, an outlet valve, a cylinder, a piston, and a chamber. When water flows into the inlet valve at a high elevation, it fills the chamber and closes the inlet valve. As the water level in the chamber rises, it pushes the piston up, which opens the outlet valve. This allows the pressurized water to flow out of the pump and into the distribution system. The cycle repeats as more water enters the inlet valve, creating a continuous flow of water without the need for external power sources.

4. Industrial Applications: Hydraulic ram pumps can also be used in industrial settings to transport water for various applications such as cooling, cleaning, or processing. They are particularly useful in areas where water is scarce or where access to electricity is limited.

Overall, hydraulic ram pumps offer a simple, efficient, and sustainable solution for transporting water in various applications, particularly in areas where access to electricity or traditional water pumping methods is limited.

prompt: What are some common misunderstandings about the causes and consequences of the 2008 global financial crisis?
response:
1. Misunderstanding the role of subprime mortgages: While the subprime mortgage crisis played a significant role in triggering the financial crisis, it is not accurate to blame it solely on these types of loans. Subprime mortgages represented only a small portion (around 13%) of the total US mortgage market at the time. The real estate bubble, lax lending standards, and the proliferation of complex financial products like collateralized debt obligations (CDOs) also contributed significantly to the crisis.

2. Ignoring the impact of regulatory failures: Many people still believe that the financial crisis was primarily caused by reckless behavior from Wall Street executives and investors. However, a lack of adequate regulation also played a major role. In particular, the deregulation of derivatives markets allowed for the creation of opaque and risky financial products that amplified the impact of the housing crash.

3. Underestimating the importance of international factors: While the initial shock came from the US, the financial crisis quickly spread around the world, causing widespread economic damage. Factors such as global interconnectedness, trade imbalances, and capital flows all contributed to the severity of the crisis. Failure to recognize this has led to a misguided focus on domestic policy solutions rather than addressing the root causes of the crisis.

4. Overemphasizing the impact of government bailouts: Some people argue that government intervention exacerbated the financial crisis by bailing out failing banks and institutions. However, studies have shown that without these actions, the crisis would have been much worse. The failure of Lehman Brothers, for example, led to a sharp contraction in credit markets and a precipitous drop in stock prices. Government intervention helped to prevent further systemic failures and mitigate the economic fallout.

5. Neglecting the long-term consequences: While the immediate effects of the financial crisis were devastating, its impacts continue to be felt today. High levels of debt and unemployment persist in many countries, and inequality has continued to widen. Failure to address the underlying structural issues that contributed to the crisis has left many economies vulnerable to future shocks. It is crucial to recognize the long-term consequences of the financial crisis and take steps to prevent similar crises from occurring in the future.

prompt: What are some common misunderstandings about the causes and consequences of the 2008 global financial crisis?
response:

Regulators failed to adequately monitor and control the risks posed by complex financial products such as collateralized debt obligations (CDOs) and credit default swaps (CDS).

3. Underestimating the impact of leverage: Banks and other financial institutions used excessive amounts of borrowed money, known as leverage, to make riskier investments. This led to a domino effect when these investments soured, causing widespread bankruptcies and losses.

4. Neglecting systemic risk: Financial institutions became increasingly interconnected through their holdings of each other's assets, creating a network of systemic risk that could spread rapidly throughout the financial system. This risk was largely ignored until the crisis exposed its dangers.

5. Failing to address income inequality: The gap between the rich and poor widened dramatically during the years leading up to the crisis. This inequality fueled reckless speculation, excessive borrowing, and other risky behaviors that contributed to the crisis.

6. Overlooking the role of globalization: The global nature of finance and trade made the crisis a truly global event, with impacts felt around the world. Policymakers failed to consider the potential risks and benefits of globalization in their decision-making processes.

7. Ignoring the importance of culture and values: The culture and values within financial institutions and the broader society contributed significantly to the crisis. A focus on short-term profits and a disregard for long-term sustainability led to risky behavior and a lack of responsibility for one's actions.

These misunderstandings highlight the need for greater understanding and awareness of the complex factors that contribute to financial crises. Addressing these issues requires a multifaceted approach that considers the interactions among various factors and takes into account both individual and systemic risks. Only then can we hope to prevent similar crises from occurring in the future.

He played a central role in the foundation of a number of co-operative dairy companies in the 1870s and 1880s before founding The Danish Butter Export Union Ltd. in 1902. He served on the board of the Port of Copenhagen from 1913 and was its vice chairman from 1926.

Early life and education
Stilling-Andersen was born on 24 June 1858 in Ølgod, the son of farmerJens Mathias Bollerup Andersen (1822–68) and Marie Cathrine Mouridsen (1827–79). Career
Stilling-Andersen played a central role in the foundation Hjedding  Co-Operative Dairy and was its first manager. In 1884, he also founded the first co-operative dairy in Sønderjylland. In 1885–89, he was manager of Nørre Nebel Co-Operative Dairy.

He was in 1889 engaged as a consultant  in  P.  A. Alberti's  Danske Landmænds Smøreksportforening. He left the enterprise in 1892 to set up his own butter export business,  et A/S The Danish Butter Export Union Ltd., with himself both as managing director and chairman.  Stilling-Andersen was a co-founder of the Danish Dairy Board (Dansk Mejeristforening) in 1887 and served on the board from 1887 to 1901.  He served on the board of the Port of Copenhagen from 1913, from 1926 as chairman.

Personal life
Stilling-Andersen married Mette Marie Christensen Tranberg (10 November 1860 - 17 May 1936), a daughter of farmer Christen Knudsen T. Stilling-Andersen was created a Knight in the Order of the Dannebrog in 1904 and was awarded the Order of Merit in 1932.

In July 2005, Gallegos was again named one of the worst legislators in Texas by Texas Monthly.  Nevertheless, Gallegos was sworn in as Governor for one day on May 5, 2007, in a Texas tradition honoring the Senate President Pro Tem.

Personal life
Gallegos attended the University of Houston–Downtown (UHD) where he received a Bachelor of Arts degree in social sciences in 2001.

On March 10, 2006, Gallegos released a statement acknowledging that he was in a one-month residential treatment program for his alcoholism. How do we see things?
When we look at an object, light is reflected from it into our eyes, which enables us to see. Light enters through the cornea, which acts like a window at the front of the eye. The amount of light entering the eye is controlled by the pupil, which is surrounded by the iris – the coloured part of the eye. The pupil changes size according to how much light is present; it is smaller in bright light and becomes larger when there is less light.

As the cornea is curved, it bends the light entering the eye, creating an upside-down image on the retina. The retina is a complex part of the eye, and its job is to turn light into signals about images that the brain can understand. Only the very back of the retina is light sensitive: this part is roughly the size of a 10p coin. It is packed with photosensitive cells called cones and rods, which help us to see in the daytime and at night.

Parts of the eye
The diagram below shows the parts of the human eye that work together to enable us to see. These include the lens, retina and the optic nerve.

Other parts of the eye include the aqueous humour, which is a liquid that sits in a chamber behind the cornea. It keeps the eye nourished and helps it maintain an optimum pressure so that the eyeball remains spherical. The vitreous humour is a clear gel that fills the space between the lens and the retina. It also keeps the eye healthy and maintains its round shape.

The sclera is the white part of the eye, forming an outer layer that protects everything inside, while the choroid is the layer of the eye that lies between the retina and the sclera. It is made up of layers of blood vessels that nourish the back of the eye.
How do we see images?
Our brain works together with our eyes to process the information we see and transform it into recognisable images. The clear disc-like part of the eye called the lens helps to focus light on the retina. The ciliary muscle adjusts the shape of the lens, helping it to focus on objects at different distances. This automatic focusing is a reflex response and is not controlled by the brain.

Once the image is clearly focused on the sensitive part of the retina, energy in the light that makes up that image creates an electrical signal. Nerve impulses can then carry information about that image to the brain through the optic nerve, which is a collection of more than a million nerve fibres. As the cornea bends light when it enters the eye, the brain receives images that are upside down, so it turns them the right way up when it processes the information.

How do we see in colour?
Cone cells located on the retina at the back of the eye are responsible for daylight vision. They enable us to see images in colour and detail. There are three types of cones, each sensitive to a different wavelength of light: red (long wavelengths), green (medium wavelengths) and blue (short wavelengths).

We can see colours other than red, green and blue because the cones can detect additional wavelengths of light and work together to produce different colours. The brain is able to interpret the signals sent from the cones into colours. It is thought that the human eye can perceive around a million colours, although people whose eyes have a fourth cone can see even more.

Rods, found alongside the cones, are responsible for night vision. They are sensitive to light but not to colour, meaning we can only see shades of grey in low-light conditions. In darkness, the cones do not function at all. Animals that are active at night can see in the dark because their eyes contain millions of additional rods.
Common eye conditions
Refractive errors are eye disorders caused by irregularity in the shape of the eye. This makes it difficult for the eyes to focus images clearly, and vision can become blurred and impaired.

Short sight (myopia) and long sight (hypermetropia) are common conditions, both caused by the cornea and lens not focusing properly on the retina. Short sight is where the eyeball is elongated or the lens is too thick, causing the image to focus in front of the retina. Long sight is where the eyeball is too short or the lens too thin, causing the image to focus behind the retina. Prescription glasses can help with both long and short sightedness.

Cataracts are the leading cause of blindness. In this eye condition, the lens becomes cloudy or less transparent, blocking light from passing through to the retina and resulting in blurred vision that can progress to blindness. There are other sight-threatening eye conditions and eye diseases that are not so easily corrected, including glaucoma and neglected tropical diseases such as trachoma and river blindness, all of which can cause blindness if left untreated.

What we’re doing to protect sight
For more than 70 years, Sightsavers has been working with partners to prevent or treat these and other causes of avoidable blindness that affect hundreds of millions of people in low and middle income countries. We do this not only by distributing treatment and carrying out operations to restore sight, but also by improving health care in local communities to enable more people to have their eyes checked, and to ensure they can be treated if they need it.

You can find out more about what we do, or support Sightsavers’ work and help people to see again by making a donation.

When we look at an object, light is reflected from it into our eyes, which enables us to see. Light enters through the cornea, which acts like a window at the front of the eye. The amount of light entering the eye is controlled by the pupil, which is surrounded by the iris – the coloured part of the eye. The pupil changes size according to how much light is present; it is smaller in bright light and becomes larger when there is less light.

As the cornea is curved, it bends the light entering the eye, creating an upside-down image on the retina. The retina is a complex part of the eye, and its job is to turn light into signals about images that the brain can understand. Only the very back of the retina is light sensitive: this part is roughly the size of a 10p coin. It is packed with photosensitive cells called cones and rods, which help us to see in the daytime and at night.

Parts of the eye
The diagram below shows the parts of the human eye that work together to enable us to see. These include the lens, retina and the optic nerve.

Other parts of the eye include the aqueous humour, which is a liquid that sits in a chamber behind the cornea. It keeps the eye nourished and helps it maintain an optimum pressure so that the eyeball remains spherical. The vitreous humour is a clear gel that fills the space between the lens and the retina. It also keeps the eye healthy and maintains its round shape.

The sclera is the white part of the eye, forming an outer layer that protects everything inside, while the choroid is the layer of the eye that lies between the retina and the sclera. It is made up of layers of blood vessels that nourish the back of the eye.

Our brain works together with our eyes to process the information we see and transform it into recognisable images. The clear disc-like part of the eye called the lens helps to focus light on the retina. The ciliary muscle adjusts the shape of the lens, helping it to focus on objects at different distances. This automatic focusing is a reflex response and is not controlled by the brain.

Nerve impulses can then carry information about that image to the brain through the optic nerve, which is a collection of more than a million nerve fibres. Cone cells located on the retina at the back of the eye are responsible for daylight vision. They enable us to see images in colour and detail. Later, Meares came to believe that it was the atavistic regression rather than the treatments that went with hypnosis that helped the patient. prompt: What is the role of a lawmaker in the US government, and what are some of the basic requirements to become a lawmaker?
response:
The primary role of a lawmaker in the United States government is to create, enact, and amend laws at the federal, state, or local level. Lawmakers are responsible for representing their constituents' interests and ensuring that laws align with the principles of democracy, justice, and equality. They also have a duty to oversee the implementation and enforcement of existing laws and provide oversight to executive branch agencies.

To become a lawmaker in the United States, an individual must meet certain eligibility requirements. At the federal level, to serve in the House of Representatives, one must be a U.S. Citizen for at least seven years, at least 25 years old, and a resident of the state they represent. To serve in the Senate, one must be a U.S. Citizen for at least nine years, at least 30 years old, and a resident of the state they represent.

In addition to meeting these constitutional requirements, most lawmakers have significant prior political experience. Many begin their careers as local elected officials, such as city council members or mayors, before moving on to higher office. Others may have served in state legislatures or worked in other roles in government or politics. A background in law or public policy can also be beneficial, as it provides a strong foundation in understanding legal and regulatory issues.

Finally, successful lawmakers must possess strong communication skills, as they regularly interact with constituents, stakeholders, and colleagues. They must also be able to work collaboratively with others, as passing legislation often requires building coalitions and negotiating compromises. Overall, becoming a lawmaker requires a combination of personal qualities, professional experience, and adherence to constitutional requirements.

prompt: What are some examples of pressure in everyday life? Provide three examples and explain them.
response:
1) Deadline Pressure: One common example of pressure in everyday life is deadline pressure. This type of pressure arises when we have to complete a task or submit a project by a specific date. For instance, let's say you have an important presentation due at the end of the week for your job. You may feel pressure to finish preparing your slides and rehearsing your speech to ensure that everything goes smoothly on the day of the presentation. Deadline pressure can be intense and stressful, but it can also be motivating as it helps us focus our efforts and prioritize our workload.

2) Financial Pressure: Another type of pressure that many people experience in their daily lives is financial pressure. This could be pressure to pay off debts, save for retirement, or make ends meet. For example, imagine that you have a significant amount of credit card debt with high-interest rates. You might feel pressure to come up with a plan to pay off the debt as quickly as possible while still covering your living expenses. Financial pressure can be overwhelming, but finding ways to manage it, such as creating a budget or seeking professional advice, can help alleviate the stress.

3) Social Pressure: Social pressure refers to the pressure we feel from others to conform to certain expectations or norms. This type of pressure can arise in various situations, such as social events, work environments, or relationships. For example, suppose you're invited to a party where most of the guests will be wearing formal attire. In that case, you may feel pressure to dress similarly, even if it's not your preferred style. Similarly, in a workplace setting, there may be social pressures to fit in with coworkers or adhere to company culture. While social pressure can sometimes be beneficial, it's essential to remember that we don't have to conform to every expectation placed upon us. Finding ways to assert our individuality and stand firm in our beliefs can help reduce the negative impact of social pressure.

prompt: What are some examples of pressure in everyday life? Provide three examples and explain them.

For instance, a student preparing for a final exam might spend countless hours studying and practicing, feeling immense pressure to perform well and achieve the desired grade.

In a romantic relationship, for example, there may be pressure to maintain the relationship, communicate effectively, and meet each other's needs. This pressure can be especially intense when one partner feels that the other isn't putting in enough effort or communicating clearly. Similarly, in a family relationship, there may be pressure to uphold certain traditions, values, or expectations. For instance, a child may feel pressure to live up to their parents' standards of success or follow in their footsteps professionally.

In all these examples, pressure can have both positive and negative effects. On the one hand, it can motivate individuals to perform at their best, pushing them to overcome challenges and achieve their goals. On the other hand, excessive pressure can lead to anxiety, stress, and burnout, potentially causing physical and mental health problems. Therefore, it's essential to manage pressure effectively, finding ways to cope with it and minimize its negative impact while still reaping its benefits.

Bonus depreciation in real estate can be a powerful tool for an investor to use to significantly reduce taxable net income.

Before we talk about bonus depreciation, let’s begin with a quick review of real estate depreciation in general. 

As IRS Publication 946 explains, depreciation is an allowance real estate investors receive for property wear and tear, deterioration, or obsolescence. A real estate investor may use an annual depreciation deduction from pre-tax income to recover the cost basis of a property over the time an investor owns a property. 

Most types of tangible property such as real estate (excluding the land value), furniture, flooring, appliances, and landscape improvements can be depreciated. 

However, a property must meet the following requirements to be depreciable:

Property must be owned by a taxpayer rather than rented
Property must be used for business or investment purposes
Property must have a determinable useful life
Property must have an expected useful life of more than 1 year.

Residential real estate used for investment purposes can be depreciated over a period of 27.5 years. If a single-family rental home has a value of $110,000 (excluding the land), the annual depreciation expense would be $4,000. 

Some items within a home can also be depreciated over a shorter period of time. For example, the IRS allows appliances and carpeting to be depreciated over a period of 5 years. 

If an investor spends $10,000 to buy new kitchen appliances and carpeting for the bedrooms, the depreciation expense would be $2,000 for the next 5 years.

The declining balance system for depreciation allows an investor to depreciate assets based on their remaining useful life. As the name suggests, larger depreciation deductions may be taken initially, and as the balance declines the depreciation expense goes down as well. 

IRS Publication 527, Residential Rental Property, provides an in-depth explanation of the declining balance depreciation system for rental real estate.

The third type of depreciation in real estate is bonus depreciation that allows a taxpayer to deduct some of an item’s cost in the first year. 

Many real estate investors may be unaware of this depreciation tax deduction that expires in a few years. So, in the rest of this article, we’ll take a closer look at bonus depreciation in real estate and how it works.

It’s important to note that bonus depreciation in real estate applies only to improvements and not to a rental property itself. 

That’s because real estate has a useful life of more than 20 years. Residential rental property is depreciated over 27.5 years, while commercial real estate is depreciated over a period of 39 years.

The 100% bonus depreciation in real estate only lasted until the end of the 2022 tax year. 

Bonus depreciation and the Section 179 deduction are 2 different types of deductions. 

While bonus depreciation is used to expense improvements to a rental property, Section 179 of the IRS tax code allows an investor to deduct the purchase price of equipment such as autos, office equipment, or computers, subject to certain limitations.

Unlike a Section 179 deduction, bonus depreciation is:

Not limited to an annual dollar amount.
Not limited to the annual profit of a business.
Item does not need to be used more than 50% of the time for business.

In other words, bonus depreciation can be claimed even if a business is not turning a profit. For real estate investors, that can be an important distinction, because sometimes a rental property depreciation expense can significantly reduce or even eliminate taxable net income.

prompt: What are the key components of an airbag system in a vehicle, and how does it work to protect occupants in a collision?
response:
An airbag system in a vehicle typically consists of several key components that work together to protect occupants in the event of a collision:

1. Airbags: These are inflatable bags made of nylon or similar materials that are designed to cushion the head, chest, and other critical areas of the body during a crash. They are deployed from compact modules located in the steering wheel, dashboard, doors, or seats.

2. Sensors: Various sensors are installed throughout the vehicle to detect impact, acceleration, and occupant presence. Some common types of sensors include accelerometers, gyroscopes, strain gauges, and pressure sensors.

3. Control module: This is the "brain" of the airbag system that processes signals from the sensors and determines when to deploy the airbags based on specific criteria such as severity of the impact, occupant position, and seat belt usage.

4. Inflator: This is a device that rapidly fills the airbag with gas (usually nitrogen) to inflate it within milliseconds of deployment. The inflator also contains a pyrotechnic initiator that ignites a chemical reaction to generate heat for inflation.

5. Diagnostic system: This component enables the airbag system to be monitored and tested periodically to ensure proper function and identify any potential issues.

When a collision occurs, the sensors send data to the control module, which then calculates whether the airbags need to be deployed. If so, the inflator is activated, causing the airbag to fill quickly and provide protection for the occupant. The airbag then deflates slowly over time to minimize discomfort and allow the occupant to exit the vehicle safely. Overall, the airbag system is designed to minimize injury and save lives by providing supplemental protection to occupants in addition to seat belts.
